section_1.title: Introduction: The Curse of Dimensionality
section_1.content: Briefly review the definition of a sphere in 2D (circle) and 3D. Introduce the concept of n-dimensional space (R^n) where a sphere is defined by the set of points at distance r from the origin: Σ_{i=1}^n x_i^2 = r^2.
section_1.example: Visual: A 2D circle morphing into a 3D sphere, then a wireframe projection representing a 4D hypersphere.

section_2.title: Scaling Geometry: Volume vs. Surface Area
section_2.content: Explain how the formulas for volume and surface area evolve as dimensions (n) increase. Introduce the Gamma function Γ(n) to generalize factorials for high dimensions.
section_2.example: Visual: A side-by-side bar chart showing that as n approaches infinity, the volume of a unit sphere actually tends toward zero.

section_3.title: The 'Spiky' Phenomenon: Where is the Volume?
section_3.content: Introduce the counter-intuitive concept that in high dimensions, almost all the volume of a sphere is concentrated in a thin 'shell' near the surface, and specifically near the 'equator' or 'corners'.
section_3.example: Character analogy: Imagine a 'High-Dimensional Orange' where the peel (the crust) contains 99.9% of the fruit's mass, leaving the center essentially empty.

section_4.title: Application: Why this matters in Data Science
section_4.content: Connect high-dimensional geometry to machine learning. Explain why distance metrics (like Euclidean distance) lose their meaning in high-dimensional feature spaces (the 'distance concentration' problem).
section_4.example: Scenario: A recommendation system for a streaming service representing user preferences as a point in a 1,000-dimensional space; explaining why most users appear to be at a similar distance from each other.

section_5.title: Conclusion: Developing Geometric Intuition
section_5.content: Summarize that high-dimensional spheres behave very differently than our 3D lived experience. Encourage learners to trust formal algebraic definitions over physical spatial visualization.
section_5.example: Visual: A final animation showing a 'cloud' of data points scattering into a high-dimensional void, highlighting the shift from visual intuition to mathematical rigor.

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2

        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject
